Let an effective geometric organization be Geo = (X, d, N, K), where X is a family of recoverable loci, d represents inherited metric organization, N represents effective neighborhoods, and K represents admissible relational couplings. A candidate spatial regime S is present when the following conditions jointly hold: 1. Joint resolvability: There exist distinct loci A and B recoverable within one effective geometric configuration. 2. Stable localization: Loc(A) and Loc(B) remain recoverable under admissible variation. 3. On the quotient 𝓔/≈ , define a strict candidate temporal precedence relation ≺ₜ by: ▪ [eᵢ] ≺ₜ [eⱼ] iff eᵢ ≺⁺ eⱼ and not(eⱼ ≺⁺ eᵢ). This quotient construction does not assume that the original dependency graph is acyclic. [...] The transitive reachability relation then supplies strict partial-order structure on the quotient [...] A temporal interpretation is still not automatic. ≺ₜ is a structural order candidate.
The methodological rule is therefore strict: latent integration may carry dependency structure before it carries duration.

A temporal order is a stable, recursively recoverable strict ordering of relational transformations derived from retained dependency, such that the ordering constrains admissible histories without requiring an external time parameter. Raw ≺ is the inherited dependency relation; ≺ₜ denotes the stronger order earned only after cycle reduction and the additional coherence conditions stated here.

A temporal chain is a set of mutually comparable quotient events under ≺ₜ. [...] A branch occurs when one event constrains more than one admissible successor. A merge occurs when one event depends on retained consequences from more than one predecessor.

▪ NC(eₐ,eᵦ) = number of retained update steps along chain C. But N is not automatically duration. [...] Counting provides a candidate precursor of duration only when the counted unit is itself stable, reproducible, and relationally accessible.

▪ K₀ ↦ K₁ ↦ … ↦ Km ≈ K₀ [...] ▪ τK(A,B) = nK(A,B) · uK. Here nK is the number of stable K-cycles occurring across the dependency interval between A and B, and uK is the conventional unit assigned to one cycle. The formula is not yet a claim that τK equals proper time.

A candidate clock K should satisfy at least four conditions: recurrence: the system repeatedly returns to a comparison-equivalent state; countability: cycles or phases can be distinguished and retained; stability: the relevant cycle structure remains sufficiently invariant across the domain of use; couplability: other processes can be compared with the clock without the comparison relation itself silently defining the desired temporal result.

▪ 𝒯 = (𝓔/≈ , ≺ₜ, Rec, Cyc) where: 𝓔/≈ is the quotient of resolvable relational events by mutual dependency reachability; ≺ₜ is the strict partial-order candidate induced by one-way dependency reachability between those quotient classes; Rec is the family of retained records or constraints by which precedence can be recovered, lettered to stay clear of the relation set ℜ of Formalism; Cyc is an optional family of recurrent comparison processes, lettered to stay clear of the configuration set 𝒞 of Formalism, that can support endogenous metric standards when they satisfy stability conditions.

A metric temporal quantity becomes defensible only if at least the following conditions can be satisfied: ordered comparability: the relevant states admit stable precedence relations; repeatable standard: a recurrent process provides distinguishable, countable cycles or phases; cross-standard calibration: independently realized recurrent processes exhibit stable comparative ratios over a regime; resolution robustness: the inferred temporal measure is not an artifact of one arbitrary decomposition into update steps; frame coherence: overlapping local frames agree on precedence where dependency is shared, even if their quantitative clock readings later differ; non-circularity: no external time variable or target relativistic behavior is built into the update rules that supposedly derive the measure. These conditions do not prove that metric time must emerge.
Remove all external iteration counters, timestamps, and manuscript-order labels. Determine whether the precedence relation can still be reconstructed from retained relational structure.
Delete or perturb a purported predecessor and test whether the admissibility or structure of the claimed successor changes in the predicted way.
Construct at least two independently organized recurrent subsystems and test whether their comparative cycle ratios stabilize without one clock being defined from the other.
Change temporal resolution and determine whether precedence and any proposed metric ratios remain stable over a finite regime.
Introduce incomparable or branching update structures and verify that the formalism does not force an artificial global total order.
Give neighboring local frames partial access to the same dependency network and test whether they recover compatible orderings on the shared portion.
Use transformation laws that are microscopically reversible and determine whether the framework incorrectly manufactures thermodynamic irreversibility from dependency notation alone.
Verify that no propagation speed, Lorentzian signature, null relation, or invariant c is required to make the temporal construction work.

The organization of jointly resolvable loci becomes spatially coordinated when the localization of one cannot be varied freely without changing the relational localization structure around it: spatial localizations are not independently assignable. Schematically: ΔL(A) ↦ Δ{d(A,B), d(A,C), N(A), …}.

Once localization classes that distinguish membership in a domain D are spatially coordinated, a relational membership boundary may be represented geometrically as ∂D: relational boundary ⇝ geometric boundary ⇝ spatial boundary. Only then do inside, outside, region, enclosure and surface acquire literal spatial interpretation.
